extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, patent practitioners, and litigants
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards for determining patent infringement of mechanical and chemical inventions, including claim construction, combinations, equivalents, improvements, and priority between patents. Focuses on when use or manufacture by a defendant amounts to infringement given the specification and claims of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cannot claim beyond method described
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee 'could not claim beyond the method actually described' in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Bovill's ventilation-vanes patent did not cover Pimm's fan-in-centre method; each inventor entitled to protection only in respect of the method disclosed in their respective specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bound to the precise claim language (literal construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee is bound to the claim as described; if the specification confines the claim to a particular form, the patentee cannot assert a broader combination than that described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: plaintiff who claimed only the combination 'with a catch-plate as described' was held bound to that limited claim; defendant not using a catch-plate did not infringe (Boyd v. Horrocks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of mechanical equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Where there is novelty in the machine and in the result produced, equivalents that produce the same result by substantially similar means may constitute infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: same intermittent radial motion produced by slightly different arrangement (shaft actuated by tappets vs. radius actuated by tappets) was held an infringement (Proctor v. Bennis). Courts will apply this doctrine when the result and means are substantially similar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule on interfering patents (priority defeats later patent)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whenever it appears that the use of a prior patent invention would be an infringement of a subsequent patent, the second patent cannot be sustained.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two patents interfere (claim same invention), the earlier patent prevails; acts under the later patent may infringe the earlier one (Pollock C.B.; Saxby v. Hennett).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent for improvement does not permit use of earlier patented features
rubrics_metrics.description: A person may patent an improvement upon an existing patent, but cannot use the improved invention before the earlier patent expires without a licence from the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the defendant's invention is a substantial improvement, use of any part of the earlier invention that is new and material (and to which the earlier patent extends) constitutes infringement (Lister v. Leather; White v. Fenn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance-and-essence test for combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: If in substance and essence the combination is taken, and the parts (or their mechanical equivalents) are so arranged as to produce the same result, then an infringement has been committed even if certain parts are omitted or added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Justice Cuttam (Parkes v. James): omissions or additions do not prevent infringement if the essence of the plaintiff's combination is appropriated; mechanical equivalents are treated as taking materially the same parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-construction dilemma: wide reading vs narrow reading
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee's claim is read widely so as to cover the alleged infringement it may be anticipated; if read narrowly to avoid anticipation there may be no infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants often force patentees into this dilemma: broad claim risks invalidity for anticipation; narrow claim risks no infringement. Cases cited: Stevens v. Keating, Dowernes v. Falcon Works, Gosnell v. Bishop, Hutchison v. Patullo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims require entire combination or its substance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a combination alone is claimed there is no infringement unless the entire combination, or the substance of it, is taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court propositions: 1) combination-only claims protect only entire combination or its substance; 2) subordinate parts/minor combinations not protected unless expressly claimed; 3) subordinate parts when claimed must be new, useful, and patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate parts not protected unless expressly claimed and patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Subordinate parts and minor combinations will not be protected unless they are expressly claimed, and when claimed must be new, useful, and patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee must make it plain in the specification that he intends protection for subordinate integers; absent express claim and patentability of the part itself, protection for parts is limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: New and material part of a combination may infringe if separately patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Taking a new and material part of a combination can be an infringement where that part is 'of itself new and useful' so as to be the subject-matter of a distinct patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier cases held new/material parts protected without express claim (Lister v. Leather), but later decisions limit this protection to parts capable of being separately patented (Tatham v. Dania; Parkes v. Stevens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential nature of invention governs infringement questions
rubrics_metrics.description: In infringement questions the essential nature of the invention will be regarded: whether what has been taken is really and substantially a part of the invention depends on how the parts contribute to the object and their relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine what parts were taken, how they contributed, and their interrelation — not decided in the abstract but by looking at the machine and its workings (Lord Blackburn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-substantial part of a combination is not infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The taking of one part out of a combination, where the part taken is not a substantial part nor capable of being the separate subject of a patent, is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Garrard v. Edge (taking a non-substantial part not infringement); Murray v. Clayton (substituting hand-power for one old mechanical part may not infringe if not substantial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture/export of parts of a combination may infringe if part is new and claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a patent is for a new combination made of old parts, manufacture of separate parts and exportation may be infringement if the part so made is new and is claimed as new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goucher v. Clayton held that making and exporting a part abroad could be an infringement where the part was new and claimed in the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple distinct heads of invention: infringement of any head actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are several distinct heads of invention in a patent, an infringement of any one of them renders the infringer liable to legal proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities: Gilbert v. Heys, and others; a patent with multiple distinct inventive features can be enforced as to each separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same legal rules apply to chemical and mechanical inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The same principles apply to chemical inventions as to mechanical: courts ask whether the new principle, new method, or new combination of ingredients discovered by the patentee has been borrowed by the alleged infringer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: cases concerning borax in cements (Stevens v. Keating), photographic processes (Talbot v. Laroche), and chemical carburet use (Heath v. Unwin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical equivalents and the date-of-knowledge test
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a chemical equivalent may amount to infringement if either the specification covers equivalents or the equivalent was known to be such at the date of the patent; if an equivalent was not known at the patent date and the patentee claimed a specific substance, later equivalents may not infringe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath v. Unwin: House of Lords held no infringement where defendant used component parts that produced carburet during operation but the patentee had claimed a specific metallic carburet and equivalents were not known at the patent date. Court examines whether patentee limited claim to particular substance and whether equivalents were known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific-material claim limits scope; different materials may avoid infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the specification confines the claim to a particular material or mode of use, the use of a different material/process may not be infringement unless the judge/jury find them to be equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Talbot v. Laroche (collodion process vs. gallic-acid-prepared paper) — jury asked whether collodion use was the same; verdict found no infringement. The court asks whether the substitute is 'the same' or a 'chemical equivalent'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of later better substitutes may be a new patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequently discovered, cheaper or better equivalent that was not known at the date of the original specification may itself be patentable; the original specification may be bad if the patentee knew of such equivalents and failed to disclose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heath v. Unwin reasoning: if the patentee had known cheaper equivalents at the time and failed to disclose, specification might be insufficient; but later discovery of equivalent can justify a new patent for that improvement.
